name: Fanonism
period: Fanon’s anti-colonial humanist and participatory programme, 1952–1961
description: An anti-colonial tradition emphasising liberation, popular political education, cooperative development and transformation of colonial social relations.

axes.brief: Mass political education and decentralised popular authority oppose a leader-centred single-party bourgeois dictatorship.
axes.counterEvidence: A revolutionary party guides mobilisation; Fanon does not supply a complete contemporary constitutional code.

axes.brief: Freedom from colonial policing and intimidation favours civil participation with protection from domination.
axes.counterEvidence: Liberation can involve coercive armed struggle; modern preventive and health mechanisms are explicit analogies, not quoted policy.

axes.brief: National culture develops through popular struggle and solidarity rather than fixed racial essences.
axes.counterEvidence: Shared national consciousness matters; Fanon criticises both empty cosmopolitan imitation and chauvinist ethnic rivalry.

qualifications.9: Common administration and recognition of distinct celebrations compete.

axes.brief: His criticism of expelling other Africans and racial-national exclusion favours mobility and solidarity.
axes.counterEvidence: This is an extension of anti-chauvinism; a contemporary visa and housing programme is not specified.

axes.brief: Armed liberation from colonial domination is compatible with human solidarity and opposition to imperial conquest.
axes.counterEvidence: Revolutionary violence is not support for every overseas campaign or automated weapon; those mechanisms remain qualified estimates.

axes.brief: National liberation should develop into African and human solidarity rather than bourgeois chauvinism.
axes.counterEvidence: Colonial international domination is rejected; independent self-determination is not automatic delegation to existing global institutions.

qualifications.7: National liberation and broader solidarity can conflict.
qualifications.13: Sovereign protection and continental mobility compete.

axes.brief: Cooperative nationalisation puts resources and intermediary trade at the service of the people.
axes.counterEvidence: Fanon explicitly rejects replacing colonial owners with a corrupt state bureaucracy; communal ownership need not mean central administration of every firm.

axes.brief: Independent productive development and escape from raw-material dependence favour selective protection.
axes.counterEvidence: International solidarity and technical exchange remain valuable; tariffs and online-service rules are less specified than rejecting neo-colonial dependency.

axes.brief: Popular planning and cooperative development should build productive capacity rather than enrich intermediaries.
axes.counterEvidence: Decentralised cooperatives and initiative qualify rigid compulsory central production targets and wage schedules.

axes.brief: Development should serve the whole population and overcome colonial privilege and concentrated wealth.
axes.counterEvidence: Tax instruments and compensation of former landowners are modern estimates; emancipation is broader than equalising cash incomes.

axes.brief: Political emancipation and common human membership oppose religious rivalries deciding civil rights.
axes.counterEvidence: Religious community life need not be abolished; festivals and private belief differ from clerical approval of legislation.

axes.brief: Colonial gender roles and inherited hierarchies can change through participation and liberation.
axes.counterEvidence: Fanon’s treatment of gender and sexuality contains tensions; modern marriage and identity curricula are qualified extensions, not a uniform published programme.

qualifications.6: Family support and emancipation from compulsory roles coexist.

axes.brief: Productive invention and technical education should replace stagnant colonial economic relations.
axes.counterEvidence: Technological development does not settle every irreversible medical or ecological risk; bounded trials and safety review are inferred.

axes.brief: The party should be decentralised and regional officials should develop popular participation.
axes.counterEvidence: Fanon also criticises wealthy regional separatism that abandons poorer regions; local authority coexists with national solidarity.

axes.brief: Colonial social institutions, language and violence shape subjectivity; racial hierarchy is a political construction.
axes.counterEvidence: Individual biological variation is not denied; exact trait proportions are less explicit than the rejection of racial destiny.

qualifications.12: Personal predispositions and social formation both contribute to temperament.

phrase: A society where formerly colonised people direct their own development through popular participation, cooperative production and solidarity beyond racial hierarchy.

religion.reason: Anti-colonial humanism and political participation do not require a particular faith; religious division is criticised as an instrument of domination.
